posts.title: Epicurus' Garden and the SF hacker house
posts.summary: Epicurus wanted friendship and a quiet mind. SF hacker houses want speed. The useful overlap is smaller: choose the room carefully, write the norms down, and leave room to recover.
posts.body:
Around 306 BCE, Epicurus bought a house and garden outside the Dipylon gate, on the road toward Plato's Academy. Diogenes Laërtius puts the price at eighty minae, writing centuries later, so treat that number the way you would any figure from one late source. What is better attested is how the place ran. People lived there. They ate at one table, argued over the food, and came back to the same unfinished questions the next week. The Academy up the road was a school you visited. The Garden was one you moved into, which changed what it could ask of the people in it.

They were after ataraxia: a quieter mind, less fear, fewer pointless wants. Friendship was part of the practice, not a networking bonus. Women studied there. So did people the rest of the city treated as background. That made the Garden unusually open for an Athenian school, but it was not casual about commitment. If you needed public honor more than the shared table, you did not last.

Epicurus's will tried to keep the group going after him. Successors named. Friends' children cared for. Freedom for slaves who had studied. The legal language is dry and that is the point. The house was supposed to outlive one charismatic man.

You see cousins of this arrangement long before anyone rented a Victorian in the Mission and called it a house for builders. Pythagoras's circle in southern Italy was harsher and weirder: shared property, heavy secrecy, intellectual heat with a mystic edge. Monasteries later made a more durable version of group life. Their purposes were religious, their rules stricter, their days split between prayer, labor, and study. They also copied books.

In 1417, Poggio Bracciolini found Lucretius' On the Nature of Things in a monastic library. Lucretius was the great Roman carrier of Epicurean thought. A Christian house preserved a poem whose gods, matter, and death sat badly with Christian teaching. Nobody needed to plan that irony. The rule said copy books, so books got copied, including ones the copyists would have disliked if they stopped to argue with every page. That is a boring reason to write shared rules down, and a strong one. Rules keep operating on days when nobody is in the mood to remember the founding pitch.

San Francisco keeps reinventing a louder cousin of the same pressure. Rent is absurd. Solo technical work is lonely. Hard problems move faster when the people who can help are down the hall instead of three Slack hops and a calendar invite away.

Reporting on HF0 describes a selective residency for technical founders in large SF properties. AGI House has been covered as a place for AI builders, researchers, dinners, and events. Those are specific organizations with their own admissions and economics. They are useful because the trade is visible. Residents give up privacy and some control over the room in exchange for people, conversation, and work being close.

Proximity helps when the people already share enough. A stuck problem can come up over eggs. Someone can watch a demo fail and still be there when the fix works at midnight. Proximity has no moral quality of its own. If residents disagree about noise, money, ambition, cleanliness, or whether every meal is a pitch session, the hallway becomes another meeting they cannot leave.

Founder mythology likes to skip the boring part. A house full of impressive résumés can be worse than a smaller one where people agree about visitors, quiet hours, chores, and rest. Size photographs well. Norms decide whether anyone wants to stay. Intensity needs a limit too. Epicurus treated modest pleasure, freedom from fear, and time among friends as the point. A modern technical residency may be trying to ship a company in weeks. Different aims. Both get worse when sleep thins, the kitchen turns strange, and small annoyances become politics.

Demigod is not a house, and we will not pretend the lineage is direct. We run a matching service for SF startups and talent: profiles stay private, both sides see evidence before names move, and an introduction happens only after each side approves. What we take from the houses is a working assumption rather than a philosophy. Selection has to be honest before proximity is worth much, because the wrong people in a good room mostly cost each other a month.

Whether any of this works outside one small city is an open question. SF is where we can check our own claims in person, so SF is where we operate.

posts.title: The letter of introduction
posts.summary: Before institutions, a vouch worked because someone with a reputation to lose spent a little of it. Evidence-first intros try to keep that, minus the network.
posts.body:
Cicero wrote a great many letters asking one busy man to receive another. The thirteenth book of his Letters to Friends is close to nothing else: a provincial governor is asked to give a trader a fair hearing, to look kindly on a young man of decent family, to not let an old friend's affairs go unattended. The Romans called it commendatio. Read a handful and the shape repeats. He names the person, says how he knows them, states plainly what he wants done, and then does the load-bearing thing: he stakes his own standing on it. If the man turned out to be a fool or a cheat, some of that stuck to Cicero.

The form is older and wider than Rome, and it kept being reinvented because it kept being needed. A letter carried a merchant into a city where no one knew his face. A written character from a former employer followed a servant into the next house. Letters of credit let a name stand in for gold across a distance that gold could not safely travel. Different goods, one move: a person who would be embarrassed by a bad recommendation spent a little of their reputation so a stranger could be treated as less of a stranger.

It is worth being precise about which part did the work, because it is easy to admire the wrong one. The value was never the paper or the seal. A claim a person makes about himself costs him nothing to make, so it carries little. A vouch from someone with standing to lose carries what the self-claim cannot, precisely because it can rebound on the voucher. The information is in the risk, not the ink.

Modern hiring mostly runs on the cheap signal. A resume is a claim about oneself, formatted well. A cold message is another. Both are easy to send and easy to inflate, and everyone on the receiving end knows it, which is why so little of either gets read. The expensive signal still exists — the warm intro from someone whose judgment you trust — but it is rationed by who happens to know whom, which is not the same as who is a fit. Talent without the right network sends cheap signals into a void. Founders drown in them.

Demigod is a matching service, not a letter of introduction, and we will not stretch the comparison. What we are trying to do is move some of the weight from who-you-know back onto evidence. A startup writes a short brief with a clear ninety-day outcome. Talent keeps one private profile. Our tech ranks the fit against that outcome, a person reviews before any name moves, and an introduction happens only when both sides have looked and both have said yes. Profiles stay private until then. The fee is ten percent, and only if a hire actually starts.

The point of the old letter was that an intro should already carry weight when it lands, so no one has to spend social capital on a coin flip. We are betting the evidence can do more of that work than a network can, and do it for people the network never reached. That is a bet, not a proof. Whether a marketplace can carry what a trusted friend's letter used to carry is exactly the thing we are in San Francisco to find out, in person, where we can be wrong about it quickly.

posts.title: The masterpiece
posts.summary: Guilds made you make the thing before they called you a master. Modern hiring runs from that test. Evidence-first matching tries to make it cheaper to ask.
posts.body:
To become a master in a medieval guild, you generally had to make a thing. Not describe it, not swear to it, not produce a witness who would swear to it for you — make it, and hand the finished object to men who made such things for a living and would judge it without sentiment. The Germans called the piece a Meisterstück, the French a chef-d'oeuvre. Our word masterpiece is the fossil of the requirement: a piece submitted to prove mastery, before the title was granted, not after.

The details varied by trade and town, and a fair amount of the surviving rules are as much about protecting incumbents as certifying skill — a guild could rig the test to keep numbers down as easily as to keep quality up. Hold that caution. But the core idea outlived every abuse laid on it, because it answered a question every craft has to answer somehow: can this person actually do the work, or only say so? A locksmith submitted a lock that had to open and hold. A cooper, a barrel that had to not leak. The object did not care about the applicant's family, his charm, or how badly he wanted it. It worked or it did not, in front of people who could tell.

That is a different kind of evidence from a good word, and worth keeping separate from it. A recommendation transfers someone else's trust. A masterpiece transfers nothing — it is the thing itself, and the judgment is made on the thing. You can inflate a claim about your work almost for free. You cannot inflate the work. The cost of faking is exactly what makes the signal worth reading.

Modern technical hiring knows this and mostly runs from it. The resume is the claim; the interview is often theater layered on the claim; and everyone has met a confident talker who could not ship. So the more careful teams reach for the object: a portfolio, a code sample, a scoped take-home, a paid trial. These are masterpieces in the old sense, and they are unpopular for an honest reason — they cost the candidate real time, and they cost the company real time to judge well. The standing temptation is to skip back to the cheap signal and hope.

Demigod does not set the test, and we will not pretend to judge anyone's craft for them; the hiring team does that, as they should. What we try to do is put the evidence in front of the right people early. A startup writes a brief with a concrete ninety-day outcome. Talent keeps one private profile built to show work, not only claim it. Our tech ranks fit against that outcome, a person reviews before any name moves, and an introduction happens only when both sides have looked and both have said yes. The aim is to spend the expensive, honest signal on the few matches worth it, rather than the cheap one on everybody.

The guilds were not utopias, and neither is a marketplace. But the old instinct had one thing right: when it genuinely matters whether someone can do the work, ask to see the work. We are betting a fair amount of San Francisco's hiring would go better if that were easier to ask for, and we are here to find out whether we are right.

posts.title: The trial year
posts.summary: The monastic novitiate was a bounded, two-sided trial: both sides tested the fit before anyone was bound. A ninety-day outcome borrows the shape.
posts.body:
The Rule that Benedict of Nursia wrote for his monasteries in the sixth century is a short, practical book, and one of its least mystical chapters is about how to let someone in. Do not receive a newcomer easily, it says. Make him wait at the door a few days. Then give him a place among the novices and test him. The tradition settled on a year for the probationary stretch, though the Rule's own timing is looser than the later custom made it. What matters is not the exact length but the shape: a bounded period of living the actual life before either side is bound to it.

The test ran both ways, and that is the part worth holding onto. The community was watching whether the newcomer could really do this — the hours, the silence, the work, the other people — not whether he could describe wanting to. And the newcomer was finding out the same thing about the place and about himself, in conditions he could not fake his way through for a year. The Rule is blunt that the point is to see whether the novice truly seeks the life, not whether he is eager in week one. Eagerness is cheap. A year of ordinary days is not.

Either side could end it. The novice was free to leave; the community was free to decline him. Nobody had signed anything permanent yet, so ending it early was a correction, not a failure — cheaper for everyone than discovering the mismatch after vows. That gap between a reversible trial and an irreversible commitment is the whole design. The trial exists precisely so the commitment can be made with less fear.

The instinct outlived the monasteries. Apprenticeships had their terms before mastery. Modern employment has probation periods, though they are often a formality nobody takes seriously in either direction. What tends to get lost is the two-sidedness — the honest version is not the company auditioning the hire while the hire pretends everything is fine. Both are supposed to be finding out, and both are supposed to be able to walk without it being a catastrophe.

Demigod is not a monastery, and a job is not a vocation. But we borrowed the shape on purpose. A startup writes a brief around a concrete ninety-day outcome — not a vibe, a thing that will or will not have happened in ninety days. Our tech ranks fit against that outcome, a person reviews before any name moves, and an introduction happens only when both sides have looked and both have said yes. Either side can pass, privately, at any point before that. The ninety-day outcome is the trial made explicit: something real to test the fit against, on a horizon short enough that a wrong match is a correction and not a year lost.

Benedict was arranging lives, and we are arranging work, which is a smaller thing. But the smaller thing goes wrong the same way when nobody builds in a way to find out early. We would rather help two people learn in ninety days what they might otherwise learn in a bad year.
